title: Spread over us
hookLine: lay us down in peace and spread over us your shelter

lines: A BLESSING THAT ASKS FOR A ROOF.
cards: For a child, the night's fear is the dark under the bed. Later the list changes. The bill on the counter.
The test result that hasn't come. The person who didn't text back. The noise downstairs.
In the daytime they're errands; after midnight, with the house quiet, they can get very loud. The evening service has a blessing for exactly that hour.
It's said every night, between the Shema and the silent prayer, and it's the one that asks for a roof.

teach.h: LAY US DOWN, RAISE US UP.
teach.b: Hashkiveinu means lay us down. The prayer begins, in plain English: lay us down, LORD our God, in peace, and raise us up again, our King, to life. Notice the pair, lying down and getting up.
It doesn't ask for a perfect night. It asks to make it through to morning. Then the central image: spread over us your shelter of peace.
A sukkah, like the booth of the festival. Not a fortress with stone walls; a light hut with leaves for a roof, where you can see the stars through the gaps. Shelter that is real, but fragile.
Then the prayer gets specific. It asks to be kept from enemies, from disease, from sword, from hunger and from sorrow, and asks God to remove the adversary from before us and behind us.
The night's fears, named one by one. The Talmud calls this blessing a long extension of the blessing about redemption that comes just before it.
Some connect it with the first Passover night in Egypt, when families stayed inside their houses while danger passed through the streets. How does it end?
On weekdays, in most communities: blessed are you, who guards his people Israel forever.
On Friday nights, the ending changes: who spreads the shelter of peace over us, over all his people Israel, and over Jerusalem.
On Shabbat, the shelter is the last word.

how: Hashkiveinu is the second blessing after the Shema in the evening service, said every night; on Friday nights its closing changes to 'who spreads the shelter of peace', and many congregations sing it.

o: lay us down: a night blessing asking for peace
a lullaby sung by parents at the bedside
rise up: a morning blessing for waking well

p: who spreads the shelter of peace

s: Hashkiveinu asks for a night with no troubles at all
it asks to lie down in peace and rise again to life.
the shelter in the prayer is a sukkah, a light booth
sukkat shlomecha: not a fortress, a covering.
the blessing ends the same way every night
on Friday nights it ends with the shelter of peace.

games.q: it's Friday night, and the leader reaches the end of Hashkiveinu. what's the last line?
o: who guards his people Israel forever.
who spreads the shelter of peace over us.
games.why: on Shabbat the ending changes: who spreads the shelter of peace over us, over all Israel, and over Jerusalem.

practice: Bring to mind the place you'll sleep tonight and picture a light roof spread over it, branches and leaves with a little starlight through the gaps, a covering rather than walls.
Under it, name one worry you'll take to bed, say it once plainly, and picture it under the roof with you, covered too.

wordCard.voice: Hashkiveinu. Lay us down. The evening blessing that asks for peace through the night, and a shelter spread overhead.

orig.note: Hebrew: your shelter of peace, from the Hashkiveinu blessing.
